source.title: Neural Networks and the Chomsky Hierarchy
source.authors: Gr'egoire Del'etang; Anian Ruoss; Jordi Grau-Moya; Tim Genewein; L. K. Wenliang; Elliot Catt; Chris Cundy; Marcus Hutter; S. Legg; J. Veness; Pedro A. Ortega

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies length generalization on algorithmic sequence tasks, but does not measure grokking over optimization time. It mentions a possible very delayed grokking effect only as something its experiments cannot rule out.
record.gate_note: Appendix B.2 reports that changing the maximum training sequence length affects length generalization on Reverse String. This is not a test of delayed test-accuracy improvement after training accuracy saturates: training uses continually sampled sequences, and the paper does not report accuracy over optimization time. The grokking reference is a caveat, not an experiment.
record.test_reason: The paper studies length generalization of sequence models on formal-language tasks with continually sampled data. It reports no train/test accuracy trajectories over optimization time, so it cannot show a delay after training accuracy saturates. Grokking (Power et al.) appears only in Appendix B.8, as a caveat: they cannot rule out 'some very delayed grokking effect'. The Appendix B.2 'phase transition' is over training range (data length), not training time.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors' main conclusion, however, is that grouping tasks by the Chomsky hierarchy predicts length generalization: RNNs and Transformers fail on non-regular tasks, LSTMs solve regular and counter tasks, and only memory-augmented networks solve CF and CS tasks. More data, steps or layers do not fix this (Table B.6). The grokking mention is a caveat that very delayed grokking cannot be ruled out.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains networks on continually sampled algorithmic sequence-transduction tasks and evaluates generalization to longer sequences; it does not use the original grokking setup or measure training-time accuracy trajectories.
record.method_sensitivity: Length generalization changes with the maximum training sequence length in the Stack-RNN Reverse String experiment.

fits_no_version.finding: Stack-RNN on Reverse String fails to length-generalize for training ranges N<10 and succeeds for larger ranges (Fig B.1). The authors attribute small-range failure to memorizing a lookup table.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Memorization versus algorithm learning in length extrapolation depends on the range of training sequence lengths (a data-diversity threshold), not on training time.

record.problems: The reported phase transition concerns length extrapolation, not delayed generalization over optimization time. The authors note that they cannot rule out results under excessive training or a very delayed grokking effect.

untested.parts: No accuracy-over-training-time curves; no delay after training saturation; no dataset-size dependence of a delay.
No progress measures or circuit formation tracked during training; the mechanism analyses (Fig 3, B.2) are of final models only.
No non-algorithmic data and no initialization-scale or weight-norm manipulation.
No weight decay is used, and there is no critical-dataset-size or ungrokking test.
Learned algorithms are inspected for some best models, but cross-run convergence is not tested in a grokking context.
No optimizer or numerical-precision controls bearing on grokking delays.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only': grokking is mentioned once, as a caveat, with no analysis. Table B.6 varies training steps (100k to 10M) for Transformers and finds no length-generalization gain. This is final-checkpoint scores only, not a grokking test, so it is not recorded as bearing on V1.

versions.untested_parts: No training-accuracy or test-accuracy trajectories over optimization; no measurement of a delay after overfitting or of how that delay varies with training-set size.
No gradual formation of a generalizing circuit or progress measure tracked during training.
No non-algorithmic data or initialization-scale/weight-norm manipulation testing grokking-like delays.
No realistic large-model pretraining or fine-tuning.
No test of weight decay or low-norm bias as an efficiency account, critical dataset size, or ungrokking.
No test of whether runs converge to the same identifiable algorithm across architectures or hyperparameters.
No controlled test of adaptive-optimizer instability or floating-point/softmax artifacts as causes of grokking.

rows.subject: Stack-RNN
rows.operation_detail: Varied the maximum training sequence length (training range) and evaluated generalization to longer sequences.

conditions.value: N < 10 versus larger ranges; Figure B.1 displays ranges 5, 7, 9, 10, 15, and 20

rows.measure: Accuracy on sequences longer than those seen during training; score averages accuracy over unseen sequence lengths.
rows.value: For training ranges N < 10, the model fails to generalize to longer sequences; larger training ranges encourage learning the data-generating algorithm.
rows.note: The authors hypothesize that small training ranges lead to memorization of a small finite language. This is a change in length-generalization performance, not a measured grokking delay.
rows.check: The row measures length-extrapolation score as a function of maximum training length (N<10 fails; larger N generalizes). Nothing is measured over optimization time and there is no fixed dataset, so it cannot show a grokking delay. 'Observed' is the wrong state for any grokking version. Baseline: chance is 50% for Reverse String.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
